solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Novelist, short drinker, welcomes turn over on piano in the Old Vic?

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it, so the drinker part comes after the piano

parts.note: JOANNA is old Cockney slang for a piano, as heard in a Victorian music hall

indicators.note: welcomes means the shortened drinker takes the next piece inside it
short means the word for drinker loses its final letter

parts.note: a toper is a habitual drinker
to roll is to turn over

explanation.surface: A writer, a little tippler, gets her turn playing the piano at the famous London theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Old Vic' looks like the theatre but means Victorian slang. 'Short' trims TOPER to TOPE, which 'welcomes' ROLL to give TROLLOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Joanna Trollope is an English writer of popular family novels, so she is an example of a novelist.

clue.text: Child gets stuck into mineral that's brownish-yellow

indicators.note: gets stuck into means the child abbreviation is pushed inside the mineral word

parts.note: ore is mineral-bearing rock

explanation.surface: A youngster becomes wedged in a seam of tawny rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy pigment whose colour is a dull brownish-yellow.

clue.text: Fool new official? They will be gutted

parts.note: an ump, short for umpire, is a sports official

indicators.note: a word that is gutted loses its insides, so only the outer letters of They remain

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a freshly appointed official as an idiot who is going to be devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' suggests bitter disappointment, but it means emptying They to TY.
explanation.definitionFit: Numpty is a Scottish and British slang word for a stupid or silly person.

clue.text: Sweet enthusiast collars American in charge of flying

parts.note: Aero is a British brand of bubbly chocolate bar, so a sweet

indicators.note: collars means the enthusiast word grabs and holds the American abbreviation inside it

parts.note: a nut is a fan or enthusiast

explanation.surface: A confectionery fan grabs a US visitor and takes command of the flight.
explanation.walkthrough: AERO is a chocolate bar sold in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeronautic is an adjective describing things relating to flight, so it fits the phrase meaning relating to flying.

clue.text: After manager's ultimate letter, see bank

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of a word is its final one, taken here from manager's

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely in Cambridgeshire is the crossword's favourite

explanation.surface: A note from the boss is followed by a visit to the financial institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a noun for money, but it is the verb, as in to bank on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on something is to count on or depend on it, the same as to trust in it.

clue.text: Steps character in Marathon describes close to camera

indicators.note: describes in its sense of drawing round means the Greek letter goes around the next piece

parts.note: lambda is a letter of the Greek alphabet, the language of Marathon

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, taken here from camera

explanation.surface: A runner in the Marathon is caught on film as he nears the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marathon' is a Greek town, so a 'character' there is a Greek letter rather than a runner.
explanation.definitionFit: The lambada is a Brazilian dance, and a dance is a sequence of steps.

clue.text: One awfully tipsy having drained last of red around pub?

definitions.text: One awfully tipsy having drained last of red around pub?

indicators.note: awfully suggests the word One is mangled into a new order
around means the shortened tipsy word goes round the pub abbreviation
having drained means a letter is emptied out of the word for tipsy

parts.note: oiled is slang for drunk

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, taken here from red

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: A drunk, having finished off the claret, wanders round the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having drained' empties the D from the tipsy word, which then goes 'around' the pub letters. Read whole, the clue also pictures the wine lover himself, so it is all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: An oenophile is a lover and connoisseur of wine, someone who could well end up tipsy after the red.

clue.text: I could have sworn tourist might say this in Paris?

definitions.meaning: the phrase is a mock apology said after using a swear word

definitions.text: tourist might say this in Paris?
definitions.meaning: a visitor apologising for poor command of the local language would ask pardon for their weak grasp of it

explanation.surface: A visitor to France confesses to bad language.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an apology for swearing, and literally a request for pardon for faulty spoken Gallic.

clue.text: Dawn follows quiet sauntering by lake with a cocktail

indicators.note: follows means the dawn word comes after the other pieces
sauntering suggests wandering about, so the word quiet is rearranged

parts.note: sunrise is dawn

explanation.surface: Someone strolls quietly beside a lake at daybreak, drink in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauntering' rearranges quiet to TEQUI.
explanation.definitionFit: A tequila sunrise is a mixed drink of tequila, orange juice and grenadine.

clue.text: Short-lived recording by male republican during repast

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
he is a male pronoun

indicators.note: during means the republican letter sits inside the meal word

parts.note: a repast is a meal

explanation.surface: A man's record plays while a Republican eats lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemeral describes something that lasts only a very brief time, transient.

clue.text: Frenzied comic in amusing clothes, making comeback

indicators.note: making a comeback means the concealed letters are read backwards
clothes as a verb means the words wrap around the letters wanted

explanation.surface: A wild comedian dressed in funny costumes returns to the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is a verb: the words comic in amusing hold CINAM, and 'making comeback' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic describes wild, frantic excitement, the same as frenzied.

clue.text: As leftovers are visible to everyone, tidy up

parts.note: U is the British film certificate meaning universal, suitable for all audiences
to neaten is to tidy up

explanation.surface: Leftover food on show should be cleared away.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating for a film anyone may watch.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftovers are food not consumed at a meal, so they are by nature not yet swallowed.

clue.text: Pets barked in long grass

indicators.note: barked means spoken out sharply, so the word for pets is said rather than spelt

parts.note: to pamper is to pet or indulge, so pets means pampers

explanation.surface: Dogs yap away in tall grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' looks like a noun for dogs, but it is the verb pampers; in a British accent it rhymes with the plains.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are South American plains covered in tall grass, and pampas grass is a tall ornamental plant.

clue.text: British organisation discussed quarter's produce

parts.note: a ring is an organised group, often criminal, such as a drugs ring

indicators.note: discussed means talked about, so the next word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a quarter's a fourth, one of four equal parts

explanation.surface: A British body talks about the yield from its district.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring forth is to produce or give birth to, as a tree yields fruit.

clue.text: Area in Albanian capital that's a hole

indicators.note: in means the area abbreviation goes inside the currency word

parts.note: the lek is Albania's currency, capital in the sense of money

explanation.surface: A district of Tirana is described as a dump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Albanian capital' suggests Tirana, but capital means money here.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is a hole or crack through which liquid or gas escapes.

clue.text: Contrarian almost finished course

parts.note: an anti is someone who opposes, a contrarian

indicators.note: almost means the phrase for finished loses its last letter

parts.note: past it means finished or no longer capable

explanation.surface: An awkward person has nearly completed the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests a racecourse, but it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are Italian starters, the opening course of a meal.

clue.text: Art school in county, not quite the greatest, seldom unoccupied

indicators.note: not quite means the county name stops just short of its final letter

parts.note: Surrey is a county south of London
Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest

indicators.note: unoccupied means empty, so only the outer letters of seldom are used

explanation.surface: A college of art in the shires, not quite the best, is rarely empty.
explanation.walkthrough: SURREY is an English county just south of London; boxer Muhammad Ali was known as The Greatest.
explanation.definitionFit: Surrealism is an artistic movement of Dali and Magritte, and a movement in art is called a school.

clue.text: Dry run one's taken in dodgy Nissan to find notorious school

indicators.note: taken in means these letters go inside the rearranged car name
dodgy means unreliable, so the letters of Nissan are rearranged

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, a dry person
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
I is the Roman numeral for one; the 's is one is

explanation.surface: A test drive of an unreliable Japanese car leads to an infamous academy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy' rearranges Nissan to SNIANS, and TTRI is 'taken in' after the S. St Trinian's is the riotous girls' school of Ronald Searle cartoons and British films.
explanation.definitionFit: St Trinian's is the fictional girls' school famous for its anarchic, unruly pupils.

clue.text: Heartless private lifted small island's torpor

indicators.note: heartless means the word for private loses its central letter

parts.note: inner means private, as in inner thoughts

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means the island word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: an ait is a small island in a river; the 's is a link meaning has

explanation.surface: A cruel soldier picks up a little island's sluggishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like a soldier, but it is the adjective INNER, cut to INER; 'lifted' turns AIT into TIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is sluggishness or a reluctance to move, the same as torpor.

clue.text: Person recruited starts to examine food chain in water

parts.note: RE is a Royal Engineer, an enlisted soldier

indicators.note: starts to means the opening letters of the next words are taken

explanation.surface: A new hire begins inspecting the marine food chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food chain' looks like one phrase, but food belongs to the wordplay. RE (Royal Engineers) is a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef is a ridge or line of rock or coral lying near the surface of the sea.

clue.text: Woman's given primary cabin on board?

parts.note: a berth is a sleeping place or cabin on a ship
A is the first letter and grade, so primary

explanation.surface: A lady is allocated the best cabin on the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as BERTH A, the name reads like the first-class cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertha is a female given name, so an example of a woman.

clue.text: Write back, attaching form for family member

indicators.note: back means the word for write is turned around

parts.note: to pen is to write
to hew is to form or shape by cutting

explanation.surface: Someone replies to a letter, enclosing a document for a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like a document, but it is a verb meaning to carve.
explanation.definitionFit: A nephew is the son of one's brother or sister, so a relative.

clue.text: Maybe tip ale over, amidst expression of disgust

indicators.note: amidst means the turned-round ale word sits in the middle of the exclamation

parts.note: fie is an old exclamation of disgust

indicators.note: over means the ale word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: ale is beer

explanation.surface: Someone knocks over a pint amid cries of revulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like a verb about knocking the ale over, but it is a gratuity.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip given to a waiter is a gratuity, something given for nothing, so an example of a gift.

clue.text: Claim by kid is idle talk, in hindsight

indicators.note: in hindsight means looking back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: gab is idle chatter

explanation.surface: A child's assertion turns out, looking back, to be mere chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: Saying it is a British children's way of claiming something first.
explanation.definitionFit: Children say the phrase to stake first claim to something, like calling dibs.

clue.text: Messenger regularly ignored old slave

indicators.note: every other letter of messenger is skipped, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: A courier kept being overlooked by the former slave.
explanation.definitionFit: An esne was an Anglo-Saxon labourer or serf, a crossword favourite for an old servant.

clue.text: Hip fixed using implant

parts.note: in means fashionable, the same as hip
set means fixed, as in set in place

explanation.surface: A hip joint is secured with a surgical implant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip' looks like the joint, but it means trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a piece set into something else, so something embedded or implanted.

clue.text: Sort of weapons I secure in wagons heading for the West

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means reading right to left, backwards
in means the I and secure pieces go inside the wagons word

parts.note: carts are wagons
to get is to secure or obtain

explanation.surface: A cowboy secures his arms in covered wagons heading out West.
explanation.walkthrough: CIGETARTS is read back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Strategic weapons are long-range arms, such as missiles, aimed at an enemy's homeland.

clue.text: Bet chap's a food writer

parts.note: Bet is a pet form of the name Elizabeth
David is any man's name, a chap; the 's is a link meaning is

explanation.surface: A man's wager is the work of a cookery columnist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bet' looks like a wager, but it is the short form of a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth David was a celebrated British cookery writer who popularised Mediterranean cooking.
